title: Did I Close the Garage Door? Smart Garage Controls That Check and Close From Your Phone
subtitle: A small add-on for your existing opener can tell you whether the garage is open and let you close it from your phone, as long as your garage has good Wi-Fi and your opener is compatible.
excerpt: If you have ever driven back home just to check the garage door, a smart garage control may help you check it from your phone. Here is how they work, what they cost and what to check before buying.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: You are halfway to the grocery store, or already tucked into bed, and the question pops up: did I close the garage door? For many of us, the only way to know is to turn the car around or pad out to the garage in slippers.

A smart garage control is a small device that works with the opener you already have. It tells your phone whether the door is open or closed, and it lets you close it with a tap, as long as the device has a working Wi-Fi connection in your garage. You do not need to replace your opener to get it.
How a smart garage control works

There are usually two pieces. A sensor goes on the garage door itself and notices when the door moves. A small hub, mounted near your opener, connects to your home Wi-Fi, which is the wireless internet signal from your router. The hub talks to a free app on your smartphone.

When the door opens or closes, the app can send you a notification, a short message that pops up on your phone screen. If the door is open and you want it shut, you press a button in the app. Consumer Reports has framed these controllers as an easier and cheaper upgrade than buying a whole new opener. That is a general point about the category, not a rating of the two products below.

What they cannot do: they are not a safety device. Your wall button, your remote and the opener's built-in auto-reverse, the feature that stops the door if something is in the way, still matter. These add-ons also depend on a steady Wi-Fi signal in the garage. If the signal is weak, a command may not go through.

items: Check that it fits your opener first. The myQ does not work with openers whose photoelectric sensors (the safety eyes near the floor) shut off after the door closes, with Chamberlain openers that have a yellow learn button made 2010 to 2021, or with any Linear opener. Use myQ's compatibility tool before you order. Meross says some Chamberlain, LiftMaster and Craftsman openers need an extra accessory.

Test your Wi-Fi in the garage. Stand where the hub would go and see whether your phone gets a solid signal. The myQ hub must be within 50 feet of your router, and the Meross works only on 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi, an older setting most routers still offer.

Ask about fees. The myQ hub page lists no monthly fee, but myQ's separate video plans are paid, from $49.99 to $149.99 a year. That page describes them for video devices and does not say whether the basic hub needs one, so read it before you buy. Meross says there is no subscription.
Look for reminder features. An alert when the door has been open too long, or an overnight reminder to close it, can help on forgetful evenings.
Plan for setup help. The sources mention a mounting height of about 6 feet for the myQ hub and a sensor wire for the Meross. Line up a family member, neighbor or installer.
Think about who gets access. Anyone with the app can open the door, so set up the account carefully and review who has guest or co-owner access in the app.

sections.content: Setting it up and using it well

For the Chamberlain myQ, the maker asks that the hub be mounted about 6 feet high near an outlet, with the door sensor on the top corner of the door. The hub needs to be within 50 feet of your Wi-Fi router. The app walks you through the steps one at a time.

The Meross involves connecting a sensor wire and testing your opener's wall-button terminals, the small screws where the wall button's wires attach. Meross's page describes a compatibility check that means shorting those terminals with pliers, which is to briefly bridge them with metal. That is a step to leave to a helper or an installer.

Once it is running, turn on the alerts that matter to you. A notification each time the door moves can be reassuring at first, and you can quiet it later if it becomes too much. If your device offers an automatic close or an overnight reminder, set a time that matches your routine.

After setup, test your opener's auto-reverse, as the notes for these products advise. If you are unsure how, check your opener's manual or ask an installer. Also expect the myQ hub to beep and flash before the door closes remotely. The myQ page cites UL 325 for this, and it cannot be turned off.
sections.label: Setup Tip

sections.content: A smart garage control will not solve everything, but it can take one small worry off the list. Check that it fits your opener, make sure your Wi-Fi reaches the garage, and get a helping hand with the installation. Then the next time that question pops up, you can check from your phone.

products.name: myQ Smart Garage Control (MYQ-G0401-ES)
products.blurb: Suits homes with most openers made after 1993 that have standard safety sensors, and Wi-Fi within 50 feet of the hub. It sends a notification each time the door opens or closes. Tom's Guide called it "an inexpensive, intuitive, and easy-to-use smart garage door opener — but it doesn't work with Amazon Alexa." One other site claims Alexa and Google support, which we could not verify, so check before buying for voice.

products.name: Smart Garage Door Opener (MSG100)
products.blurb: May suit people who want reminders, with an overtime alert, an overnight reminder to close the door and an optional auto close, and no subscription fee. It needs 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi, and some Chamberlain, LiftMaster or Craftsman openers need an extra accessory that Meross says it ships free in the US and Canada.
